title: Weekly POC Sync — Invoke Stability & Escape Hatches
summary: Weekly check-in to review POC results for app integration: SDK invoke patterns, function/tool calling reliability, structured output failures, and escape-hatch strategies. SE walked through logs, highlighted two reproducible failure modes (timeout vs schema mismatch), and proposed batching and KV-cache tweaks. Next steps: run a 48-hour soak in staging, share security docs, pricing estimate, and schedule a latency benchmark this Friday.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-08
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Ava (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Maya (Lead ML Eng), Ethan (Platform Eng), Sofia (PM)

[00:00] Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. We wanted to do a quick pulse on the POC this week — focus on invoke stability and escape hatches, right?
[00:12] Maya: Yeah, thanks. We had a couple of incidents overnight where function calls returned malformed JSON, and the app went into error state. We captured logs but want help understanding whether it's on our side or the model/SDK.
[00:24] Daniel: Right — quick note, some of the transcripts you shared look like schema mismatch where the response truncated mid-JSON. Could be an early token cutoff or streaming boundary in the SDK.
[00:36] Ethan: For us it's timing — the UI will wait 2s for a tool call, then attempt fallback logic. When the response is partial the parser throws.
[00:49] Sofia: Also want to prioritize graceful degradation. If the model fails, we can show cached card or call a simpler microservice.
[01:03] Daniel: Totally. Two things to consider — 1) enforce structured output with strict schema checking and server-side repair attempts, 2) implement an "escape hatch" which will either call a smaller, faster quantized model or use cached prefix responses.
[01:20] Maya: Is there a recommended pattern to repair truncated JSON? We've tried naive "wrap and ask to finish" but it sometimes hallucinated keys.
[01:31] Daniel: We've seen better results with token-aware requests: set max_tokens appropriately, add an end-of-structure sentinel, and on truncation, re-invoke with the last KV cache pointer so the model continues rather than re-generating from scratch. SDK supports resume calls, but it's opt-in.
[01:47] Ava: Quick clarification: when you say resume, that's in our hosted flow or only for Dedicated?
[01:53] Daniel: Both — runtime supports incremental KV continuation in hosted and Dedicated. For Private deployments there's a config toggle but same API surface. Sometimes the client SDK needs to pass the 'resume_token' header.
[02:07] Maya: We didn't see resume_token in our client logs — likely our wrapper dropped it.
[02:11] Ethan: Confirmed, our middleware strips unknown headers. We'll update the passthrough.
[02:18] [small crosstalk]
[02:25] Daniel: On the timeout side, we saw a cluster of tail latencies around 1.8s when sequence length spiked. Batching kept avg latency good, but tail suffered.
[02:38] Maya: We have tests that mimic long sequences for diagnosis — good to know it's the tail not median.
[02:43] Daniel: For tail, suggested levers: reduce batch-size for latency-sensitive routes, configure per-route max_batch_delay_ms, and enable prefix KV caching for repeated prompts. That will bring down token count per invocation.
[02:58] Sophia: If we shrink batch size won't cost per-token go up? There's a cost/latency tradeoff we must accept.
[03:05] Ava: That's a common tradeoff — we can show you a cost delta with the proposed settings. We'll include that in the pricing update.
[03:12] Maya: Another failure mode: we saw ‘function calling’ return a non-callable name sometimes, like the model produced 'open_file' when our tool is 'open_document'. Pretty noisy.
[03:24] Daniel: Yep. Function name canonicalization is brittle. Two options: 1) strict schema enforcement server-side — reject non-exact matches and surface a deterministic fallback; 2) a small normalization layer in the client that maps synonyms. Both can be done quickly.
[03:40] Ethan: Might prefer the client mapping first, easier to rollout.
[03:44] Daniel: Agreed. We'll supply a starter mapping table.
[03:48] [Pause]
[03:55] Sofia: On security — can you remind us where keys live and KMS story? We need to present to compliance.
[04:03] Ava: Short answer: hosted maintains keys in a KMS and we support customer-managed keys for Dedicated and Private. We'll attach SOC2 summary and KMS integration notes after the call.
[04:12] Maya: Also, data residency — can the VPC be provisioned in us-east-1?
[04:17] Ava: Yes, we have a region there. For Private we can on-prem or region-specific VPC.
[04:23] Ethan: For the soak plan: we'd like to run a 48-hour run that simulates our weekday peak pattern, including tool invocation bursts. Any caveats?
[04:33] Daniel: Ensure your test harness attaches resume tokens and reproduces the exact streaming boundaries. We'll monitor server-side metrics and provide a per-route token and latency breakdown.
[04:44] Maya: Great. On structured output enforcement — is there an SDK helper that will attempt to re-serialize when the JSON is malformed?
[04:52] Daniel: There's a lightweight helper in the SDK v0.9.x that will try to safely close unbalanced braces or extract the last complete JSON object. It's heuristic, not perfect. For mission-critical paths we recommend a two-step approach: parsing attempt -> if fails, attempt resume with a small prompt asking for 'complete the last object' with strict schema instructions -> if still fails, apply escape hatch.
[05:14] Sofia: Can you capture that flow in a short runnable snippet? That will help our devs.
[05:19] Daniel: Yes — I'll paste a Node/Python snippet in the thread.
[05:22] Ava: Let's also talk about fallback model options. If a full-size model fails, what's the recommended secondary model?
[05:28] Daniel: We typically recommend a 7B quantized variant for the escape hatch — good latency, lower cost, and often preserves structured output well. We also have tuned quantized checkpoints that favor conservative outputs.
[05:40] Maya: Any observed regressions when dropping to 7B for structure? We've seen missing optional fields in previous runs.
[05:47] Daniel: There can be missing optional fields. That's why we recommend a prioritized field strategy: required fields are validated; optional fields can be populated by a deterministic post-processor (e.g., default values or a small rule-based filler).
[05:58] Ethan: For billing, if we fall back are we billed for both? Curious about double billing on retries.
[06:05] Ava: Good question — we bill per-token across the runtime. If you issue a resume continuation it's additional tokens; fallbacks incur tokens for that invocation. We'll show cost modeling so you can set budgets and thresholds.
[06:16] [short pause]
[06:22] Maya: We ran into an odd edge-case where the SDK automatically retried a 500 and re-sent the same streaming request, causing duplicate tool side effects. Any guardrails?
[06:33] Daniel: SDK has an idempotency token you can pass per request. On server side we dedupe tool-calls if token matches and within TTL. Looks like your middleware wasn't setting it.
[06:44] Ethan: We'll add idempotency token generation in our gateway.
[06:47] Sofia: On observability — can we get token-level cost and model route traces in the console for the pilot?
[06:55] Ava: Yes we can grant increased retention for your pilot routes and share a per-route dashboard. We'll attach a sample trace and walk you through it.
[07:04] Maya: Anything else on tuning?
[07:07] Daniel: Quick checklist: set per-route max_batch_delay to 10ms for low-latency routes, isolate long-sequence routes to separate worker pool, enable KV prefix caching for repeated prompts, and tune max_tokens to avoid mid-output truncation. Also consider a fallback policy that triggers on x% schema failure rate within y minutes.
[07:29] Sofia: Let's call out success criteria if we were to move to Dedicated — SLO targets?
[07:34] Ava: For Dedicated we can contract for median p95 under 300ms for short sequences and p99 under 800ms depending on commit. We'll get formal numbers in the pricing doc.
[07:47] Maya: We want to be sure the structural regressions reduce below 0.5% of calls before rolling to prod.
[07:54] Daniel: That's reasonable. As we tune caching and batching, we should see that drop.
[07:58] Ava: Ok let's recap actions — Daniel to run the benchmark, Maya to share failing transcripts, Ava to send pricing and security docs, Ethan to provision VPC and add idempotency tokens.
[08:12] Ethan: Confirmed. Also will do the header passthrough fix for resume_token.
[08:18] Daniel: I'll also attach the small normalization table for function names and the SDK snippet for JSON repair.
[08:25] Sofia: Sounds good — would like a mid-week quick sync if soak shows anomalies.
[08:30] Ava: We'll ping for that. Thanks everyone.
[08:35] [call ends]

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-attributed lines and minor gaps where audio overlapped; some product names transcribed incorrectly (e.g., 'resume token' sometimes shown as 'resume tokin').
questions: What is the recommended pattern for repairing truncated JSON responses?
How should we implement escape-hatch to a quantized model with minimal cost impact?
Can we get SOC2 summary and KMS integration notes for compliance review?
Will fallback retries cause double billing and how to estimate costs?
Can idempotency tokens be applied to prevent duplicate tool side effects?
